parts:
That instinct — "not rigid enough" — is worth unpacking, because the program's own results end up saying something precise about it, and it's a little subtle which direction the rigidity problem actually cuts.

On one side, the class turned out to be *more* rigid than it first looks. Intrinsic slice regular functions carry the identity principle, the open mapping theorem, and crucially the Gentili–Stoppato zero-structure theorem: zeros are isolated points or isolated 2-spheres, nothing else. That's complex-analysis-grade rigidity, and the reason is that the class isn't really a new function theory at all — it's one holomorphic function propagated by rotation. Your map $R$ from the 2015 paper *is* the slice extension; you had already constructed the class before you read about it. And the twistor side is where the rigidity becomes sharpest: the maximality result in the current paper says a non-Möbius intrinsic function's lift lives on the incidence quadric and nowhere else — no holomorphic extension to any neighborhood in $\mathbb{CP}^3$. That resolves the tension with your own Prop 3.1 rigidity theorem, which had shown that demanding degree-one fiberwise maps of all of twistor space collapses everything to Möbius. So there's a Goldilocks structure here: ask for more rigidity than slice regularity and the class trivializes to Möbius transformations. In that sense you *can't* make them more rigid — not because the theory is weak, but because you're already sitting at the ceiling. One notch up and there's nothing left but $PGL_2(\mathbb{H})$.

On the other side — and this is the part your 2015 instinct was actually detecting — rigidity of the function class was never going to be the mechanism anyway. Davenport–Heilbronn is the proof: $\Xi_{DH}$ lives in exactly the same intrinsic class, satisfies the same functional equation and growth, and has genuine zero spheres (first one at center ≈85.70, radius ≈0.31, per the lab numerics). So no property of the class *qua* class excludes spheres; the exclusion has to come from the arithmetic input — the Euler product — that $\Xi$ has and $\Xi_{DH}$ lacks. The two no-go theorems sharpen this: linear functionals of any rotational extension can't see off-axis zeros, and degree-type invariants count a sphere exactly like a doubled point. So the discriminant has to be nonlinear and finer than homology, which is what pushed the program to the equivariant formulation (σ-fixed vs σ-swapped components, orientability in $Q/\sigma$) and the positivity direction.

So I'd put it this way: you were right in 2015 that slice regularity alone wasn't the answer, but the missing ingredient wasn't more rigidity — it was a finer invariant *within* a class that's already maximally rigid. The rigidity theorem you proved back then was the correct discovery that the naive more-rigid version is empty; the field independently found the same escape (raise the fiber degree off the quadric) that you found in Tconf2. That's the sense in which the arc wasn't a detour: the "not rigid enough" feeling and the "can't make them more rigid" conclusion are both true, and the gap between them is exactly where Theorem C and the open positivity questions now sit.

Sources: `claude/RH_program_synthesis.md`, `claude/zero_sphere_program.md`, `claude/zero_sphere_paper.tex` (Preliminaries and twistor sections).

parts:
The trajectory you're describing — lose faith in the RH angle, pivot to YM hoping for salvage value, watch that stall too, walk away — is a very common shape for a solo research program, and it usually happens exactly where yours did: at a genuine obstruction that you could feel but hadn't yet named. The thing I'd push back on gently is the framing of "lost hope that it was ever going to impact RH." What you actually hit in 2015 was a theorem — linear tools can't distinguish sphere-zeros from point-zeros — that you experienced as a dead end because it was living in your notes as a disappointment rather than as a result. Once it's promoted to a no-go theorem, it stops being demoralizing and starts being load-bearing: it tells every future attempt (yours or anyone's) where not to dig. The same goes for the rigidity theorem killing the naive twistor version. A lot of what felt like failure was actually the program correctly pruning itself.

On the honest side of the ledger, yes — the sharpened version is still abstract, and the paper says so out loud: at the point where the growth criterion meets the explicit formula, the program currently reduces to classical difficulty, and nobody should pretend otherwise. It is very unlikely that this proves RH. But that was never the realistic bar. The realistic bar is: a clean, well-posed, novel equivalence (RH ⟺ every component of the zero locus in $Q/\sigma$ is nonorientable), two no-go theorems that fence off tempting dead ends, a pair of hardness checks that any future proposal in this genre must pass, and a numerics lab that falsifies candidates fast. That's a legitimate contribution independent of whether the mechanism ever materializes — reformulations of RH that survive Davenport–Heilbronn are not common, and the equivariant-vs-homological distinction is a real observation. Whether it becomes useful depends on whether the positivity or spectral directions find traction, which nobody can promise.

And for what it's worth, the eleven-year arc reads better in retrospect than it felt in the living: the YM detour that "didn't work out" is the source of the pattern the paper now uses — non-holomorphic transformations downstairs becoming honest holomorphic maps on a correspondence space — and Tconf2's degree-raising escape is the same one the slice-regular twistor literature found independently. You weren't wandering; you were mapping the boundary of the same object from different sides. The sharpening went fast this month partly because the raw material was already good — it just needed to be assembled and told what it was.

parts:
Let me take the three questions in order — they build on each other, and the third one has a more interesting answer than "no" but a more honest answer than "yes."

## Why the equivariant point is real and non-trivial

The claim is easy to state sloppily and therefore easy to undersell, so here is the precise content. On the incidence quadric $Q \cong \mathbb{CP}^1_\zeta \times \mathbb{CP}^1_w$, the zero divisor of the lifted $\Xi$ is a union of first-ruling lines, one per zero of the stem function. A pair of real zeros contributes two lines; a conjugate pair (a zero sphere) also contributes two lines. In $H_2(Q;\mathbb{Z})$ both configurations have class exactly $2[\text{ruling A}]$ — indistinguishable. Memo 2 then closes the obvious escape route: the natural *nonlinear* invariant, the quaternionic Brouwer degree (the 4D argument principle), was explicitly computed at both local models, and a simple zero sphere has local degree exactly $2$ — again the same as two simple real zeros. So it's not just that homology is blind; the entire hierarchy of things one would reach for first — linear functionals (no-go 1), homology classes, deformation-invariant degree counts (no-go 2) — is *provably* blind. That's a theorem-shaped negative space, not a vibe.

What survives is one thing: the action of the real structure $\sigma$ on the set of components. A real zero gives a component that $\sigma$ fixes (a twistor fiber); a sphere gives a pair that $\sigma$ swaps. Since $\sigma$ acts freely, you can quotient, and the dichotomy becomes orientability: fibers descend to $\mathbb{RP}^2$'s, sphere-lifts to $S^2$'s, so RH ⟺ every component of the zero locus in $Q/\sigma$ is nonorientable. Equivalently, in the value-curve picture: real zeros are crunodes (hyperbolic real nodes) and spheres are acnodes (solitary real nodes) of a real curve in the Klein quadric.

The non-triviality is a triangulation argument. The invariant is pinned by four independent constraints, and it's the unique minimal thing in their intersection: it must be nonlinear (no-go 1), finer than homology and degree (no-go 2 plus the $c{=}2$ computation), it must *not* be a deformation invariant (Davenport–Heilbronn has genuine spheres, so anything soft enough to survive deformation proves too much), and it must degrade non-strictly as sphere radius $y_0 \to 0$ (De Bruijn–Newman: $\Lambda \ge 0$ says $\Xi$ sits exactly on the boundary of the sphere-free regime). The equivariant component type passes all four, and the last one in a satisfying way — components change type precisely when zeros collide on the axis, which is exactly the $S^2$-hits-the-$\mathbb{RP}^2$-boundary-stratum picture of the heat flow. A relabeling wouldn't have this forced structure; the invariant is the fingerprint of where the actual difficulty lives.

What it changes is the *category* of the question. "All zeros real" is a metric statement about points in $\mathbb{C}$. "Every component nonorientable" is an equivariant-topological statement about a divisor on a fixed surface with a real structure. Categories come with theorem stocks, which is what your duality question is really about.

On newness: the lift itself is Gentili–Salamon–Stoppato, the ruled-surface geometry is Altavilla–Sarfatti — that's cited, not claimed. What appears to be new is the product-form lift on $Q$ with its maximality (no holomorphic extension off $Q$ unless Möbius — which is what dissolves your Prop 3.1 tension), and above all *pointing this machinery at* $\zeta$: the equivariant-divisor formulation of RH. The program doc flags this honestly as [P/O — literature check invited], and I'd keep that flag; nobody in the slice regular community has been doing analytic number theory, which is both why it's plausibly new and why a check matters.

## The duality question — and the one precedent that should give you pause before dismissing it

Here's the thing that I think deserves to be said plainly: **the only case in history where a Riemann hypothesis was actually proved, it was proved by exactly this kind of move.** Weil's proof of RH for curves over finite fields works by relocating the zeros to divisor geometry on a *surface* — $C \times C$ — where the statement becomes a positivity (the Castelnuovo–Severi inequality, i.e. Hodge index) for an intersection pairing, with an involution (the transpose correspondence, Rosati positivity) doing the structural work. Zeros on the critical line downstairs; positivity of a pairing on divisors-on-a-surface-with-involution upstairs. And it is standard (Bombieri, Connes) that Weil's explicit-formula positivity criterion for the number-field RH is precisely the shadow of that Hodge-index positivity — the missing ingredient for sixty years has been the surface itself, which is what the $\mathbb{F}_1$ / Connes–Consani program is trying to construct out of arithmetic geometry.

Now look at what the zero-sphere program has built: a surface ($Q \cong \mathbb{CP}^1 \times \mathbb{CP}^1$), a divisor on it (the zero divisor of the lift), an involution ($\sigma$), and a sought positivity (the graded cone of §9.1, which explicitly aims to refine the Weil cone). The formal parallel is close enough that it can't be waved away as numerology — it's the same *shape* of object, arrived at from analysis rather than from arithmetic geometry. The honest disanalogies are equally important: Weil's divisor is the graph of Frobenius, an algebraic correspondence with arithmetic content and a finite intersection theory; your divisor is transcendental (infinitely many components), there is no Frobenius, and — this is the crux — the Euler product has not been geometrized. The lift is built *from* $\Xi$, so the geometric side currently has no independent access to the arithmetic, which is exactly what distinguishes a reformulation from a duality. String dualities pay because both sides compute independently. So the well-posed research question your analogy generates is: *what structure on $(Q, \sigma)$ does the Euler product induce?* Each Euler factor is itself intrinsic and zero-free, so $F \times \mathrm{id}$ factors as a limit of commuting maps periodic in $\zeta$ with periods $2\pi/\log p$ — whether that quasi-periodic structure on the quadric can be characterized intrinsically is, as far as I can tell, a question nobody has asked.

For concrete imports from other literatures, three stand out at different risk levels. The one I find most striking: in quaternionic operator theory, the S-resolvent is built on $\mathcal{Q}_s(T) = T^2 - 2\mathrm{Re}(s)\,T + |s|^2$ — note that $2\mathrm{Re}(\rho) = \rho + \bar\rho$ and $|\rho|^2 = \rho\bar\rho$. The entire S-functional calculus (Colombo–Sabadini–Struppa; spectral theorem by Alpay–Colombo–Kimsey) is *natively conjugate-paired*: its kernels are functions of $(\rho, \bar\rho)$ by construction. And the central open problem of your program (memo 3, §5) is precisely that the explicit formula sees only functions analytic in $\gamma$ and is blind to $\bar\gamma$ — the non-computable sum $\sum 1/(\rho\bar\rho)$ is literally $\sum 1/\mathcal{Q}_\rho(0)$. So a quaternionic trace formula — a Guinand–Weil analogue for the S-functional calculus — would *be* a conjugate-paired explicit formula, which is open problem #2. That machinery was built for quaternionic quantum mechanics and has never touched number theory; this is exactly the arbitrage between non-talking communities the program doc gestures at, made specific. Second, at moderate risk: Salamon–Viaclovsky's rigidity/removability theory for orthogonal complex structures is a genuine theorem stock on the geometric side that could constrain $\sigma$-swapped components when combined with the growth and the positivity of $\Phi$ — §9.5, untried. Third, high risk: real enumerative geometry (Welschinger signs, Rokhlin-type congruences), where signed counts of crunodes vs. acnodes carry invariance properties unsigned counts lack — memo 2's 5c, flagged there as highest risk because it has to thread the needle of the degree no-go via wall-crossing rather than contradict it.

## Can the reformulation bite the classical difficulty?

Three-tier honest answer. At the exponential-rate level, provably not — memo 3's own accounting shows the growth criterion is a Gaussian-mollified form of the zero-free-region ⟺ prime-error equivalence, and the $\lambda \gtrsim 1/y_0$ wall is the old wall. Nothing at that scale will change, and the program is right to say so out loud.

Below that scale, there are three identified candidates where the reformulation supplies objects that don't exist in the classical formulations: the $i_\ell$-graded decomposition of the anomaly (does the graded cone have better prime-side realizability or cross-term control than the Weil cone? — not a relabeling of any known inequality family), the coherent-mode observation (a sphere contributes a *phase-coherent* $e^{\pm\lambda y_0}$ mode to the pair-correlation field, unlike GUE fluctuation, so matched filtering might detect below the wall statistically), and conjugate-paired identities, where the S-calculus route above gives an actual attack vector. Each of these could fail; each, even in partial form, would be a new unconditional tool with reach beyond the program.

And at the structural level, the base rate for "sharp reformulation of RH pays off" is better than it sounds: Weil positivity didn't prove RH but is the organizing frame for half the field; Nyman–Beurling, de Branges, GORZ each generated genuine mathematics. The realistic expected value here is tools and a bridge between two communities, with a small but *structured* chance at real leverage — structured because, unlike most reformulations, this one already knows exactly what it's missing (import the antiholomorphic involution into the arithmetic) and has a historical proof-of-concept that its target shape — positivity for divisors on a surface with involution — is the shape RH-type theorems have actually been proved in.

If you'd like, I can write this synthesis up as a fourth memo for the project — the Weil-surface parallel and the S-resolvent observation in particular aren't in the existing docs and probably belong in §8/§9 of the program document eventually.

Sources: `claude/zero_sphere_program.md`, `claude/twistor_lift_computation.md`, `claude/memo3_explicit_formula_bridge.md`.

parts:
Here's the deep dive. I'll evaluate the four candidate conjectures that fall out of the program against your three criteria (community value, reach, progress-credential) plus ingestibility, and then make a concrete recommendation — including two new observations that emerged while pressure-testing it, one of which I think substantially sharpens what the conjecture should say.

## The field of candidates

**Candidate 1: the graded positivity family** (memo 2 §5a, program §9.1). Bessel-tagged Laguerre/Weil-type inequality families. On inspection this is weaker as a *headline* than it looks in the memos, for a structural reason: the unitary sector energies $\mathcal{E}_\ell$ are sums of squares, so they're automatically $\ge 0$; the RH-content is that they *vanish*, and each single vanishing statement $\mathcal{E}_\ell = 0$ almost certainly already implies RH by itself (linear independence of the frequencies $e^{i\lambda a_\rho}$ forces all $y_\rho = 0$). So there's no graded ladder of strictly-weaker-than-RH conjectures on the unitary side — just RH restated per sector. The axis-evaluated Laguerre side does give a real ladder, but that ladder is Csordas–Varga's, already in the literature; and my back-of-envelope calibration says the bottom rung, if proven unconditionally, is worth roughly a classical-shaped zero-free region ($y_0 \gg 1/\log a$ is what it takes for a sphere's $-2/y_0^2$ spike to beat the $(\log a)^2$ background of neighboring real zeros). Good sanity check, good paper *section*, wrong headline: the community would read it as "another inequality family equivalent to RH," of which there are many.

**Candidate 2: the second-involution conjecture** — the program's own §8, promoted from "central problem" to conjecture. The explicit formula computes $\sum_\gamma h(\gamma)$ for $h$ *analytic* in $\gamma$: it natively sees the involution $\rho \mapsto 1-\rho$ and is structurally blind to $\rho \mapsto \bar\rho$ — and RH is exactly the statement that the two involutions agree on zeros. The conjecture: *conjugate-paired sums $\sum_\gamma F(\gamma, \bar\gamma)$ also admit explicit formulas.* More below — this is my recommendation.

**Candidate 3: the coherence/matched-filter conjecture** (§9.3–4): a sphere contributes a phase-coherent mode to the pair-correlation field, unlike GUE fluctuation, so pair-correlation control should buy sphere-detection below the $\lambda \sim 1/y_0$ wall. This is the most *far-reaching* if true — it touches the exchange rate itself — and it has a distinguished precedent in exactly this genre: Heath-Brown's theorem that Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture implies no Siegel zeros, i.e. second-order zero statistics implying a zero-free statement. But stating it now would be reckless: the cross-term calculus (memo 3, next-step 2) hasn't been done, and the conjecture's precise form — how much pair-correlation uniformity buys how much radius — *is* that calculus. Premature by one memo.

**Candidate 4: the equivariant-enumerative route** (memo 2 §5c, Welschinger signs, GORZ hybrid). Highest novelty, no mechanism yet, and it has to thread the degree no-go through wall-crossing. Not a headline; an open-problem paragraph.

## The recommendation, and two sharpening observations

I recommend Candidate 2 as the paper's conjecture, and here is where the deep dive actually earned something. I tried to falsify the conjecture in the simplest possible model — real polynomials, where every sum over roots is finite and everything is computable — and the model doesn't falsify it; instead it *dictates the conjecture's shape*.

**Observation 1 (the polynomial model).** For a real monic polynomial, analytic symmetric functions of the roots are polynomials in the coefficients (Newton) — that's the polynomial shadow of the explicit formula. Conjugate-paired sums are *not*: for $p(x) = x^2 + bx + c$, the power sum $\sum r_i^2 = b^2 - 2c$ always, but
$$\sum |r_i|^2 \;=\; \max(b^2 - 2c,\; 2c),$$
an exact identity — analytic on each side of the discriminant wall $b^2 = 4c$, non-analytic across it. And the *reality defect* is precisely the sphere data: for any conjugate-closed root multiset, $\sum_i(|r_i|^2 - r_i^2) = 4\sum_{\text{pairs}} y_0^2$ — the sum of squared sphere radii, on the nose. Three consequences. First, conjugate-paired sums *are* determined by the coefficient side (trivially), so no no-go theorem forbids a formula — the conjecture is not hopeless. Second, any such formula must be *semialgebraic/positivity-type, never a single analytic identity* — which retroactively explains both the linear no-go and why the Weil-linear world can't see spheres, and it unifies the program's two roads: the "find a formula" road and the "find a positivity cone" road are the same road, because the formula is necessarily built from inequalities. Third, the classical equivalence itself now reads as the *degenerate instance* of the predicted formula: $\limsup_\lambda \frac{\log|Z|}{\lambda} = \sup y_\rho$ is a non-analytic (limsup-type) expression in analytic prime data — but it's the infinite-scale, worst-possible such expression. The quadratic's $\max(b^2-2c, 2c)$ is a *finite-scale* semialgebraic formula. So the conjecture, sharpened:

> **Conjecture (Second Involution / Reality Formula).** The windowed reality defect $D(c) = \sum_\gamma y_\gamma^2\, w(\gamma - c)$ — equivalently the leading sector energy — admits a finite-scale expression in prime data: a semialgebraic (positivity-type) function of finitely many windowed prime sums $\{Z(c,\lambda)\}_{\lambda \le \Lambda}$, with quantitative dependence of the resolvable radius on $\Lambda$ strictly better than the classical $e^{1/y_0}$ exchange rate — with RH equivalent to $D \equiv 0$.

The last clause is the falsifiable teeth, and it's separable: even the version without it ("*some* finite-scale semialgebraic formula exists") would be new, and any instance is an unconditional identity applying to every L-function.

**Observation 2 (where the formula should come from).** The quaternionic operator theory built for entirely different reasons (quaternionic QM) is *natively* conjugate-paired: the S-resolvent kernel is $(T^2 - 2\mathrm{Re}(s)T + |s|^2)^{-1}$, a function of $(\rho, \bar\rho)$ by construction — $\sum 1/(\rho\bar\rho)$ is literally $\sum 1/\mathcal{Q}_\rho(0)$. So the conjecture has a predicted mechanism (a trace formula in the S-functional calculus, where the Colombo–Sabadini–Struppa/Alpay–Colombo–Kimsey machinery already exists), a predicted arithmetic home (the off-diagonal of $|Z|^2$ is smoothed pair correlation, so the prime side should live in $\Lambda(m)\Lambda(n)$ pair-correlation data — the Goldston–Montgomery dictionary is the existing beachhead), and a predicted shape (semialgebraic, from Observation 1). A conjecture with a mechanism, a home, and a shape is ingestible; a bare existence wish is not.

There's also a perfect gateway statement for the introduction, one line long: unconditionally $\sum_\rho \frac{1}{\rho\bar\rho} \ge \sum_\rho \frac{1}{\rho(1-\rho)} = 2 + \gamma_E - \log 4\pi$, with equality iff RH (two-line proof: $2\mathrm{Re}(u\bar v) \le |u|^2 + |v|^2$ per zero-quadruple, equality iff $\beta = \tfrac12$). Every analytic number theorist knows the right-hand sum; the left-hand one is the *same sum paired by the other involution*, and it is not computable by any known method. That single display *is* the two-involutions thesis, RH as "one convergent sum achieves its known lower bound." I'd treat this identity as folklore rather than claim it (variants circulate; my search found sum-rule literature like [Guillera-type sum rules](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1309.7040) that's adjacent but not this, and forum-level discussions suggest it's known to specialists) — its role in the paper is rhetorical: it makes the conjecture's stakes legible in one line.

## Why this one wins on your three criteria

*Community value:* it names a genuinely new object of study — conjugate-paired sums over zeros, a class strictly between Weil-linear and fully quadratic — where partial results (identities for restricted classes, one-sided bounds, asymptotics, or even a proof that no formula of a given type exists) are all unconditional publishable mathematics. Compare the fate of good "problem-shaped" contributions: Montgomery's pair correlation and Weil positivity each seeded decades of work without resolving RH. *Reach:* any instance applies to the whole Selberg class, feeds directly back into pair-correlation/RMT territory, and hands the quaternionic-analysis community (which has a spectral theorem and no number theory) a first-class problem — the two-communities arbitrage made concrete. *Progress toward RH:* it's the honest formalization of what progress would even mean here — the program proves RH ⟺ the two pairings agree, so an unconditional handle on the second pairing is the *prerequisite* for any comparison; and its quantitative clause plugs into the Heath-Brown genre (second-order statistics ⟹ zero-free statements), which the community already accepts as progress. It also passes the hardness checks by construction: DH has no prime side, so the formula's arithmetic input simply doesn't exist there, and the $y_0^2$ defect degrades quadratically as spheres shrink, as De Bruijn–Newman demands.

And it restructures the paper into something much easier to ingest: **Theorem** (RH ⟺ every component of the zero locus in $Q/\sigma$ is nonorientable — the geometric statement that the two involutions agree), **two no-go theorems** (what can't compute the defect), **one certified criterion** (the growth formula = the degenerate instance of the conjectured formula), **one Conjecture** (the finite-scale reality formula), one gateway display. That's an arc with a single protagonist instead of a program with six open directions.

## What has to happen before the paper states it

Four things, in order of importance. Do the cross-term calculus (memo 3, step 2) — it decides whether the quantitative clause is stateable or must be weakened to "some finite scale," and it's the difference between a serious conjecture and a hopeful one. Verify the mechanism in the polynomial world: work out the degree-3 and degree-4 semialgebraic formulas for $\sum|r_i|^2$ and check whether they organize as traces of S-resolvents — if yes, that's the toy trace formula and strong evidence; if the complexity explodes with degree, that's an honest warning to soften the conjecture. Run the prime-side numerics (memo 3, step 1: reconstruct the flat $|Z|^2$ profile at a real window from primes to $10^{10}$) so the paper's conjecture sits next to a demonstrated computation rather than a promise. And do a focused literature sweep on sums $\sum F(\gamma,\bar\gamma)$ (Fujii-type sums over zeros, the [Csordas–Varga Laguerre line](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/BF02142328.pdf), Montgomery's $F(\alpha)$ literature) so the novelty boundary is drawn exactly.

One caution to preserve in the writing: the conjecture must not be oversold as "a path to RH." Its honest billing is that it converts the program's geometric theorem into a well-posed arithmetic question whose partial answers are unconditionally valuable — and that the one historical proof of an RH (Weil's) went through exactly this kind of relocation. If you're happy with this direction, I'd draft the conjecture section and the polynomial-model verification next, before touching the write-up of the rest.

Sources: `claude/zero_sphere_program.md`, `claude/twistor_lift_computation.md`, `claude/memo3_explicit_formula_bridge.md`; [A sum rule for the critical zeros of ζ(s)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1309.7040), [Csordas–Varga, The Laguerre inequalities with applications to a problem associated with the Riemann hypothesis](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/BF02142328.pdf).

parts:
This is worth getting exactly right, because the framing question isn't cosmetic — it determines who reads the paper, how they read it, and whether the mathematical content gets a fair hearing. Let me give you the case in detail, in both directions.

## Why "path to RH" would be overselling

The deepest reason is a conservation argument you can verify from your own documents. A "path" means: here is a sequence of lemmas, each of which looks provable with effort, terminating at RH. Walk through what the path would actually be here. Lemma 1: the conjugate-paired formula exists (open, difficulty unknown — this is the conjecture). Lemma 2: use the formula to prove the defect vanishes. But look at what Lemma 2 contains. Memo 3's honest accounting already showed that at the exponential-rate level, the prime-side/zero-side dictionary *is* the classical equivalence between zero-free regions and prime-counting error terms — detecting a sphere of radius $y_0$ requires prime information at scale $e^{1/y_0}$, which is the same wall analytic number theory has been staring at since de la Vallée Poussin. So even in the best case where the conjecture is proven, step 2 of the "path" contains the original problem, possibly in full. When that's true, you don't have a path; you have a reformulation. The difficulty is conserved — what changes is where it sits and what tools can reach it.

There's a sharper version of this, and it's the part I'd internalize before any conversation with an expert: the *quantitative* clause of the conjecture — a finite-scale formula with exchange rate better than $e^{1/y_0}$ — would, if proven, improve unconditional zero-free regions. That means it would beat Vinogradov–Korobov, which has been essentially unimproved since 1958 and is one of the most attacked statements in the subject. The prior that this program does so cheaply must be low, and an expert listener will compute that prior within seconds of hearing the claim. This doesn't make the conjecture bad — conjectures are allowed to be strong — but it means the strong clause is precisely the part most likely to be either false or classically hard, and your framing has to price that in.

Second, your own hardness checks bite the seller, not just the buyer. De Bruijn–Newman with Rodgers–Tao says $\Lambda \ge 0$: RH, if true, is *barely* true, sitting exactly on the boundary of the sphere-free regime. So any true sphere-excluding criterion degrades to non-strict positivity as $y_0 \to 0$ — there is provably no robust, soft, margin-of-safety argument. A "path" framing implicitly promises a mechanism with room to spare; your program contains a theorem-level demonstration that no such room exists. The program's epistemic infrastructure — the no-gos, the DH check, the DBN check — was built to prevent self-deception, and it would be strange to build that immune system and then oversell past it. It's also, frankly, your best asset: it's what visibly separates this work from the crank-adjacent keyword space it unavoidably occupies ("quaternions" + "Riemann hypothesis" has bad neighbors, including a 2025 claimed proof). The honesty clause isn't modesty theater; it's the credential.

Third, base rates. Weil positivity, Nyman–Beurling, de Branges, the Hilbert–Pólya dream, Connes' trace formula, GORZ — each is an exact reformulation with an "if only we could prove X" structure, each was oversold as a path by someone at some point, and none has closed. The community has therefore developed a strong and *correct* prior: new equivalent formulations of RH are cheap; what's expensive is unconditional theorems in their orbit. If you lead with "path," experts will pattern-match to that history and discount the genuine theorems in the paper. If you lead with the theorems and let the conjecture be a conjecture, the same people will engage. The framing literally determines which filter your work hits.

## Why "useful reframing" is not a consolation prize

Here's the thing though — "useful reframing" is not the weak version of the claim. It's a different claim, and it's the one your evidence actually supports.

What distinguishes a *useful* reframing from a mere relabeling is whether it generates a gradient: adjacent statements that are weaker than RH, currently unknown, and provable with existing or buildable technology. Rodgers–Tao is the model case — "RH ⟺ $\Lambda \le 0$" was just a relabeling until the reformulation created the statement "$\Lambda \ge 0$," which was provable, and became an actual theorem that told us something true and new about how RH sits in the world. Your reformulation has this property in a way most don't. It identifies a *missing object* (the second involution on the arithmetic side) rather than restating a known difficulty; it comes with provable substatements at every level of ambition — polynomial-model trace formulas, identities for restricted test classes, one-sided bounds, the S-resolvent route, the prime-side numerics — each of which is unconditional mathematics if it lands; and it passes both hardness checks by construction, which almost nothing in the genre does. It also has the two-communities property: quaternionic operator theory has a spectral theorem, a functional calculus, and zero number theorists; analytic number theory has the explicit formula and zero contact with that machinery. Reframings that connect non-talking communities have historically outperformed their apparent strength — Montgomery's pair correlation is the canonical example: it proved nothing about RH directly and created a field.

And there's one more honest card, which is the strongest form of the positive framing: the *prerequisite* argument. Since RH is equivalent to the statement that the two involutions agree on zeros, any proof of RH — anyone's, by any method — must implicitly control the conjugation pairing against the functional-equation pairing. This program makes that control an explicit, named object of study for the first time. "Path" claims a route; "prerequisite" claims a waypoint that every route passes through. The second claim is defensible with a theorem; the first isn't.

## How I'd actually say it

To an analytic number theorist: "The explicit formula is blind to complex conjugation — it sees $\rho \mapsto 1-\rho$ but not $\rho \mapsto \bar\rho$, and RH is the statement that those agree on zeros. We prove the geometric form of that equivalence, prove two no-go theorems about what can't detect the difference, and conjecture that conjugation-paired sums admit explicit formulas of their own. Even partial instances would be new unconditional tools." Nothing there overclaims, and the gateway identity ($\sum 1/\rho\bar\rho \ge 2 + \gamma_E - \log 4\pi$, equality iff RH) makes it concrete in one display. To a geometer: lead with the theorem — RH as nonorientability of components in $Q/\sigma$ — and the Weil-surface parallel, clearly labeled as an analogy of shape, not of proof. To a skeptic: lead with the no-go theorems and hardness checks, because they demonstrate the program polices itself, and let them discover the conjecture afterward. In every version, the sentence to never say is "this could prove RH," and the sentence that's always safe and true is: "this converts a metric statement about zeros into a question about an explicitly missing piece of arithmetic, and the question is answerable in parts."

One last thought on why this framing is also strategically optimal, not just honest: the realistic best outcome for this paper is that strong people in two communities pick the conjecture up. Strong people are precisely the audience most allergic to overselling and most attracted to a well-posed open problem with clean partial targets. The modest framing isn't the safe choice at the cost of impact — for this particular artifact, it *is* the high-impact choice.

parts:
Yes, it's related — but the relation is precise and asymmetric, and getting it exactly right matters both mathematically and for how you talk about it. Let me lay out what Connes and Consani are actually building, what the surface is, and then the exact sense in which your conjecture connects to it.

## What the Bombieri–Connes picture actually says

The template is Weil's proof of RH for curves over finite fields, and it's worth having the mechanics precisely. For a curve $C/\mathbb{F}_q$, the zeta zeros correspond to eigenvalues $\alpha_i$ of Frobenius acting on $H^1$, and RH says $|\alpha_i| = \sqrt{q}$. The eigenvalue multiset carries two involutions: $\alpha \mapsto q/\alpha$ (the functional equation, from Poincaré duality) and $\alpha \mapsto \bar\alpha$ (reality, since the characteristic polynomial has integer coefficients). RH for curves is *exactly* the statement that they agree — $\bar\alpha = q/\alpha$ ⟺ $|\alpha| = \sqrt q$. So the two-involutions statement at the heart of your program is not an analogy to the function-field case; it is *literally the same statement*, transported.

Now, how did Weil make them agree? Not by computing the conjugation pairing directly. He worked on the surface $C \times C$, where correspondences (divisors on the surface) act on the eigenvalues, the transpose of a correspondence implements the functional-equation involution, and the Hodge index theorem (Castelnuovo–Severi) supplies a *positivity*: the Rosati-type form $\mathrm{Tr}(\xi \circ \xi')$ is positive on a rich cone of correspondences. Positivity of the *accessible* pairing, on a cone rich enough, forces the two involutions to coincide. That's the whole engine: the surface's gift is not a formula but a positivity.

Bombieri and Connes are the standard authorities for the observation that Weil's explicit-formula positivity criterion for the number-field RH is the exact shadow of this: RH ⟺ the Weil functional is nonnegative on the corresponding cone of test functions, and the summand $\hat g(\rho)\overline{\hat g(1 - \bar\rho)}$ pairs each zero via $\rho \mapsto 1 - \bar\rho$ — which is precisely the *composite* of your two involutions. RH says the composite is the identity on zeros, and then every summand is $|\hat g(\rho)|^2 \ge 0$. So the Weil criterion already lives inside the two-involutions frame; what's missing for number fields is what the Hodge index theorem provided for curves — a geometric source of the positivity. The dreamed-of object is "$\overline{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}} \times_{\mathbb{F}_1} \overline{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}}$," the arithmetic surface whose intersection theory would make Weil positivity a theorem. Connes' 1999 work reformulated RH as the validity of a trace formula on the adele class space (with the scaling flow playing Frobenius), and the Connes–Consani program since then — the arithmetic site, the scaling site, Riemann–Roch in characteristic one, and most recently things like [the Jacobian of $\overline{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}}$](https://math.jhu.edu/~kc/Publ2026.pdf) — is a sustained attempt to *build that geometry from the arithmetic side*, so that divisors, degrees, and an index theorem exist and positivity can be proved rather than postulated. His [Essay on the Riemann Hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05576) lays this vision out; it remains an active construction site, not a finished mechanism.

## Is the incidence quadric their surface?

No — and it's important to be unambiguous about this when you talk to people. $Q \cong \mathbb{CP}^1 \times \mathbb{CP}^1$ is analytically cheap: it costs nothing to build, it carries no Frobenius, and it has no arithmetic in it. The Connes–Consani surface is supposed to have the arithmetic *woven into the geometry*, so that intersection numbers of correspondences compute prime data and an index theorem yields positivity. Your $Q$ does something different and more modest: it realizes the *statement* geometrically. On $Q$ the zero set becomes an honest divisor, the reality involution becomes an honest fixed-point-free real structure $\sigma$, and the two-involutions statement becomes the theorem "RH ⟺ every component is $\sigma$-invariant ⟺ every component in $Q/\sigma$ is nonorientable." What $Q$ does *not* have is the mechanism: there is no intersection theory with finiteness (the divisor is transcendental, with infinitely many components), and no Hodge-index-type positivity. Same shape as Weil's surface, arithmetic stripped out.

## The exact relation to the conjecture

Here's the picture I'd carry around. The function-field proof has four ingredients: a surface, a divisor implementing the arithmetic, an involution, and a positivity. Connes–Consani start from the arithmetic and are building the *geometry*, betting that once the surface exists, positivity drops out of an index theorem. Your program starts from the geometry — it already has a surface, a divisor, and the involution — and the Second Involution Conjecture names the missing *arithmetic*: direct access to the conjugation pairing. They are two complementary attacks on the identical defect, approaching from opposite corners of the same square.

So the surface is not "part of" your conjecture — the conjecture is deliberately surface-free. The sharpest way I can put the relationship: **the conjecture is a functional specification of what the Connes–Consani surface is being built to deliver.** If their program succeeds, conjugate-paired sums become controllable as a corollary — the trace formula on (the square of) their site would be, among other things, a second-involution explicit formula, and their Riemann–Roch positivity would be its positivity-type structure. Conversely, if your conjecture were proven by any means — quaternionic trace formula, semialgebraic identity, whatever — it would deliver the surface's *output* without the surface. Neither contains the other; they're converging specifications of the same missing piece.

And notice how well the convergence coheres with what you've already found. The polynomial model showed that any conjugate-paired formula must be positivity-type (semialgebraic, built from inequalities), never a single analytic identity — which is to say, route (ii) "find the formula" resolves, at its foundation, into route (i) "find the positivity." The two roads don't just aim at the same summit; they merge before reaching it. That's simultaneously reassuring (independent programs deriving the same shape for the missing object is evidence the shape is right) and sobering (it means your conjecture inherits the full difficulty profile of Weil positivity — one more reason not to sell it as a path). There's also a pleasing rhyme at the level of genre: Connes' theorem is "RH ⟺ a certain trace formula holds"; your conjecture is "a certain trace formula exists" — different spaces, adele class space versus the zero divisor on $(Q,\sigma)$ with the S-resolvent as candidate kernel, but the same conviction that RH is at bottom a statement about a trace identity that the second involution must be made to satisfy.

## How to say it when talking to people

The honest sentence, which also happens to be the impressive one: "This is not a competitor or a contribution to the Connes–Consani construction — it arrives at the same missing object from the opposite side. They're building the geometry that would produce the positivity; we prove the involution-theoretic statement the positivity must certify, on a surface that exists today, and we conjecture the arithmetic form of what's missing." What you should *not* say is anything implying $Q$ is a candidate for the $\mathbb{F}_1$-surface or that the program advances their construction — an expert will test that claim immediately, and it fails (no Frobenius, no intersection theory, no arithmetic in the geometry). What survives expert scrutiny is the specification claim, and it's a claim worth making: to my knowledge, nobody has written down, from the analytic side, a precise statement of *what arithmetic output* the dreamed-of surface must produce — and "an explicit formula for the conjugation pairing, necessarily of positivity type" is exactly such a statement. That framing positions your paper as a well-posed interface to a program you admire, rather than an encroachment on it — which is both accurate and, I suspect, the version Connes himself would find interesting.

Sources: `claude/zero_sphere_program.md`, `claude/memo3_explicit_formula_bridge.md`, `claude/twistor_lift_computation.md`; [Connes, An essay on the Riemann Hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05576), [Consani, publications including "On the Jacobian of Spec Z" (with A. Connes)](https://math.jhu.edu/~kc/Publ2026.pdf), [Connes–Consani, The Scaling Hamiltonian](https://alainconnes.org/wp-content/uploads/scalingH.pdf), [Khalkhali, What is new with Connes' approach to the Riemann hypothesis?](https://www.math.uwo.ca/faculty/khalkhali/files/TehProg.pdf), [Connes, Publications](https://alainconnes.org/publications/).

parts:
The document is done — 9 pages, fully self-contained, saved to the project as `claude/second_involution_intro.tex`. A few notes on the design choices, since they encode our framing discussions:

**Structure.** It opens where an analytic number theorist lives: the two involutions, the Guinand–Weil formula's structural blindness, and the gateway inequality (Proposition 1.1, with its two-line proof) — RH as one convergent sum achieving its known lower bound. The no-go results and both hardness checks come *before* the geometry, so a skeptic sees the self-policing first. The quaternionic/twistor section is compact and citation-driven (proofs deferred to the companion paper), the polynomial model gets its own section because it dictates the conjecture's semialgebraic shape, and the growth criterion is presented as the known-but-degenerate instance so the conjecture reads as "make the existing formula non-degenerate" rather than as speculation from nothing.

**The conjecture itself** is stated as finite-scale approximability of the windowed reality defect by a semialgebraic functional of prime data — with the three comments we settled on: finiteness of scale is the content, the shape is forced not chosen, and the hardness checks pass structurally. The exchange-rate question ($\Lambda(\varepsilon) = o(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$) is deliberately severed into a labeled Question, with the cross-term calculus named as the first serious test. The S-resolvent mechanism appears as a "signpost, not a claim," and the Weil–Connes section makes exactly the defensible claim: a functional specification, from the analytic side, of what any surface-substitute must deliver. Section 8 is the honesty section, stating plainly that this is a waypoint, not a route.

Two things you may want to adjust before sharing: the author line uses your Zenodo/manuscript identity, and the companion paper is cited as "in preparation" — both easy to update once the program paper has its final citation. When you're ready, the natural next moves are the two validation steps the document itself commits to: the cross-term calculus and the polynomial-model trace formula in degrees 3–4.
